title: Roadmap 06: DSA graphs, heaps and tries
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: Heaps (top K, median of a stream), graph traversal, topological sort, shortest paths (Dijkstra, 0-1 BFS, Bellman-Ford), union-find and tries for longest prefix match.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: You read n numbers from a stream and need the K largest at the end using only O(K) memory. Which approach runs in O(n log K) time?

options.text: Keep a max-heap of all n numbers and pop it K times at the end.
options.why: That needs O(n) memory, which breaks the stated limit.

options.text: Keep a min-heap of size K and evict the smallest when it grows past K.
options.why: Right: the root is the K-th largest so far, and each push or pop is O(log K).

options.text: Sort all n numbers in descending order and take the first K of them.
options.why: Sorting costs O(n log n) time and holds every number in memory.

options.text: Keep a sorted array of size K and insert each new number into it.
options.why: Each insert shifts up to K items, giving O(nK) time overall.

questions.explanation: The same min-heap idea merges K sorted lists: push each list head, pop the smallest, push that list's next node. In Java use PriorityQueue (min-heap by default).

questions.prompt: True or false: Python's heapq module implements a min-heap, so the usual way to get max-heap behaviour for numbers is to push negated values.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: negate on push and negate again on pop.

options.text: False
options.why: It is a min-heap; there is no max-heap switch to flip.

questions.explanation: heapq.heappush and heappop work on a plain list with the smallest at index 0. For tuples, push (-priority, item). In Java, use new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder()) for a max-heap.

questions.prompt: Design a structure with add_num(x) and find_median() over a stream of numbers. Which design gives O(log n) inserts and an O(1) median?

options.text: One min-heap of all numbers, where the median is always the root.
options.why: The root of a min-heap is the minimum, not the middle value.

options.text: A sorted array found by binary search, inserting at the located position.
options.why: Finding the spot is O(log n), but shifting items makes an insert O(n).

options.text: A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half.
options.why: Right: the median is one root or the mean of both roots.

options.text: A hash map of value counts, scanning the keys to locate the middle one.
options.why: Scanning the keys makes find_median at least linear.

questions.explanation: Rebalance after each insert so the two heap sizes differ by at most one. This is the two-heaps pattern.

questions.prompt: A grid has several gates (0), walls (-1) and empty rooms. Each room must get the number of steps to its nearest gate. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Run a separate BFS from every empty room until it finds a gate.
options.why: Correct but wasteful: it repeats work for every room.

options.text: Push all gates into the queue at distance 0 and run one BFS.
options.why: Right: the first time a room is reached is its shortest distance, in O(rows * cols).

options.text: Run a DFS from each gate and keep the largest distance seen.
options.why: DFS does not find shortest paths, and the largest value is the wrong one.

options.text: Run Dijkstra with a heap because each room has a different cost.
options.why: Every step costs 1, so plain BFS is enough without a heap.

questions.explanation: Multi-source BFS starts with all sources in the queue. The same trick solves rotting oranges and nearest-zero distance. BFS gives shortest paths only when every edge costs the same.

questions.prompt: Select all statements about Kahn's topological sort that are true.

options.text: It repeatedly removes nodes with in-degree 0 and lowers the in-degree of their neighbours.
options.why: Right: a queue holds the nodes that are ready.

options.text: If fewer than V nodes are removed, the directed graph contains a cycle.
options.why: Right: nodes on a cycle never reach in-degree 0.

options.text: It runs in O(V + E) time using a queue and an in-degree array.
options.why: Right: every node and edge is handled once.

options.text: The resulting order is always unique for a given acyclic graph.
options.why: Several valid orders usually exist when nodes are independent.

questions.explanation: Use it for course schedules and build order. For cycle detection in a directed graph you can also run DFS with white/grey/black states.

questions.prompt: Select all statements about shortest-path algorithms that are true.

options.text: Dijkstra can fail with a negative edge, because a node is treated as final when popped but a later negative edge might shorten its path.
options.why: Right: the greedy "popped means final" argument needs non-negative weights.

options.text: Bellman-Ford handles negative edges and can detect a reachable negative cycle, in O(V * E) time.
options.why: Right: if a V-th round still relaxes an edge, there is a negative cycle.

options.text: For a path with at most K stops, run Bellman-Ford for K + 1 rounds, reading distances from a copy of the previous round.
options.why: Right: the copy stops one round from chaining several edges.

options.text: 0-1 BFS uses a deque, putting zero-weight neighbours at the front and one-weight ones at the back, in O(V + E).
options.why: Right: it keeps the deque ordered by distance.

options.text: Adding the same constant to every edge to remove negatives keeps the shortest path unchanged.
options.why: Paths with more edges get penalised more, so the best path can change.

questions.explanation: Pick the algorithm by edge weights: BFS for equal weights, 0-1 BFS for 0 or 1, Dijkstra for non-negative, Bellman-Ford when negatives exist or hops are limited.

questions.prompt: True or false: a union-find structure without path compression or union by rank still guarantees near-constant find time.

options.text: True
options.why: Without those two optimisations the guarantee does not hold.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: repeated unions can build a long chain, so one find may take O(n).

questions.explanation: With path compression and union by rank or size, the amortised cost per operation is O(alpha(n)), the inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant. Typical uses: connected components and Kruskal's MST.

questions.prompt: A router has many IPv4 prefix routes such as 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.0.0/16 and must find the longest matching prefix for each destination address. Which structure keeps lookup cost independent of the number of routes?

options.text: A hash map from exact destination addresses to the next hop.
options.why: It only matches full addresses, not prefixes.

options.text: A list of all routes, scanned in order, returning the first match.
options.why: The scan grows with the route count and the first match may not be the longest.

options.text: A balanced BST of routes sorted by network address, searched for equality.
options.why: An equality search does not find a covering prefix.

options.text: A binary trie over the address bits, tracking the last route node seen.
options.why: Right: walking at most 32 bits gives the longest match.

questions.explanation: Each route marks the trie node at the end of its prefix. Lookup follows the destination's bits and keeps the deepest marked node seen, so the cost is O(32) for IPv4.
